abstract: This analysis combines AI occupational exposure measures with a novel "adaptive capacity" index to assess which workers face the greatest risk of job displacement and earnings losses. Of 37.1 million U.S. workers with high AI exposure, 26.5 million possess above-median adaptive capacity and are well-positioned to navigate job transitions, while 6.1 million workers (4.2% of the workforce) face both high AI exposure and low adaptive capacity, concentrated in clerical and administrative roles and concentrated in smaller metropolitan areas, particularly in the Mountain West and Midwest.
keyFindings: Of 37.1 million U.S. workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 26.5 million have above-median adaptive capacity and strong means to adjust to potential job displacement.

6.1 million workers (4.2% of the workforce) face both high AI exposure and low adaptive capacity due to limited savings, advanced age, geographic isolation, and narrow skill sets, with approximately 86% being women.

Medical secretaries and administrative assistants (831,000 workers), office clerks (2.5 million), and secretaries and administrative assistants (1.7 million) represent the largest occupations in the high-vulnerability category.
Highly AI-exposed workers concentrated in tech hubs such as San Jose and Seattle show the greatest concentration of high exposure coupled with high adaptive capacity.

Vulnerability concentrations of highly exposed and low-adaptive-capacity workers range from 2.4% to 6.9% across metro areas, with highest concentrations in college towns and state capitals in the Mountain West and Midwest.
methodology: Analysis combining data from seven sources: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) 2022-2024 panels for net liquid wealth; American Community Survey (ACS) 2024 for age distributions; Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) 2024 for wages and employment; Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Projections (2024-2034) for growth rates; Lightcast 2023 for geographic employment distribution; O*NET Database 30.1 (2025) for skill transferability; and Eloundou et al. (2024) AI exposure data for LLM exposure measures. The adaptive capacity index is computed at the occupation level using four standardized components: net liquid wealth, growth-weighted skill transferability, geographic density, and age. The final dataset covers 356 occupations representing 95.9% of the U.S. workforce. Occupations included only if meeting strict data quality thresholds of ≥15 SIPP respondents.
qualifiers: The adaptive capacity index is computed at the occupation level, which masks substantial variation in adaptive capacity among workers within the same occupation. The index represents an initial attempt to measure adaptive capacity and may be sensitive to alternative calculation approaches. Evidence underlying adaptive capacity estimates derives primarily from localized displacement events rather than large-scale occupational shifts, and the measure may be less informative in scenarios where AI affects clusters of related occupations simultaneously. Significant uncertainty remains about the extent to which AI will impact labor markets and the differential burdens for affected workers. If AI fundamentally transforms the economy on a scale comparable to the industrial revolution, it could make entire skill sets redundant across occupations simultaneously. The adaptive capacity index represents one snapshot in time based on available data and could change substantially as AI impacts skill demands. The index focuses on factors influencing ability to find new jobs and post-reemployment earnings, not the full range of welfare costs from job displacement such as job insecurity or loss of meaning from work.
